video.title: The Magic of the Non-Dominant Side on the Forehand

classification.reason: The coach provides executable cues to internalize the non-dominant side action, specifically 'hold the shoulder' and feeling the inward pressing action during the swing.

problem.title_as_question: How does the non-dominant side function to stabilize the forehand?
problem.definition: Understanding and executing the active inward pressing action of the non-dominant chest and arm, which balances rotational momentum and achieves a proper tucked elbow position.

quotes.text: Look at the forehand K ends this point with. Strange, right? His arms actually crossed.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, how is this going to help my forehand? Well, the left side of your chest, it actually presses back across the body on every forehand
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: normally you can't see it because that initial rotational explosion that starts the swing, it sends the left side out with momentum
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and then that pressing action where the left side presses back in. The net effect is just this elbow tuck rather than an actual press back across
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: because that outward vector is getting cancelled out by the inward vector. You're only going to see the arms actually cross on forehands with minimal rotation
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, if you didn't press at all though, it would look like this. And all of the sudden, oh, okay, you can see that doesn't look like a very well balanced forehand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And that inward pressing action is necessary to get that tucked elbow position that you see everyone play the forehand in.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Lorenzo Mousetti is a great one to look at for this because he occasionally hits these running down the line forehand winners.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: because he cuts off that rotation a little bit early on those to hit that down the line target, you can actually see that left arm across pressing action
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You can actually see that hand appear on the other side of his torso.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: That early rotational explosion that sends the elbow out and then that pressing action that finishes the swing that sends it back in
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, there are two cues, two ways to internalize this depending on what feels more intuitive for you.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: One is the literal action that's happening, which is hold the shoulder. So, as you swing, we don't want to let this happen. We want to hold that shoulder.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The second one, and this is my favorite because I think more people find it intuitive, is it will feel like you're pressing like this
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: even on your regular forehands where rotation cancels out most of that inwards momentum.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And that's because without pressing, you get this. And that pressing action for most people, their brain thinks it's doing this
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: watch how expertly he uses his left side to control his forehands and overheads.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The forehand appears off-balance without the proper tucked elbow finish of the non-dominant side.
The non-dominant arm and shoulder fly open and flail outward during forward swing rather than holding position.

causes.statement: The left side of the chest must actively press back across the body to oppose outward rotational momentum.
The initial rotational explosion that starts the swing sends the left side outward with strong momentum.
Failing to actively press inward leaves outward momentum unchecked, destroying stroke balance.

angles.summary: The outward vector from torso rotation is cancelled out by the active inward vector of the chest press, producing a net elbow tuck.
Lorenzo Musetti visibly crosses his non-dominant arm across the torso when cutting off rotation early on running down-the-line forehands.
The coach demonstrates how a forehand without inward pressing looks completely unbalanced with an uncontrolled non-dominant arm.
Even though full rotation makes the arm appear just tucked, the player's brain should subjectively feel an active crossing or pressing action.

solutions.summary: Use the cue 'hold that shoulder' as you swing to prevent the non-dominant shoulder from opening wildly.
Feel as though you are actively pressing your non-dominant arm and chest across your body during the regular forehand swing.
